paragraphs.text: Glucosephosphate isomerase (GPI) deficiency causes hereditary nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia. In his review, Arnold (1979) noted that GPI deficiency was first reported in 1967 and that patients from all over the world have a typical nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia with hemolytic crises during acute infections. Some patients also have neurological involvement, including myopathy and mental retardation (Schroter et al., 1985; Kugler et al., 1998). Paglia and Valentine (1974) also reviewed hereditary GPI deficiency.

paragraphs.text: Hutton and Chilcote (1974) described 8 children (5 living and 3 deceased) from 2 families in Kentucky and Indiana with severe hereditary nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia caused by GPI deficiency. All of the affected children were severely anemic in early life. The 3 deaths occurred in young patients who did not receive adequate blood transfusions or whose parents would not permit splenectomy. Growth and development were surprisingly normal, and no patient died of infection.
